blocks.prompt: The Shark With a Hammer for a Head
blocks.text: A hammerhead shark has a head shaped like a wide, flat hammer. Its eyes sit far apart, one on each end. This helps it see almost all the way around. The bottom of its head is covered in tiny holes. The holes feel electricity. Every animal makes a tiny bit of electricity when it moves. A stingray can hide under the sand, but it cannot hide its electricity. So the hammerhead swings its head over the sand, slow and low, until it feels something down there. Then it digs.

blocks.prompt: The Shark That Swings a Metal Detector
blocks.text: Picture someone walking a beach with a metal detector. They swing it side to side, listening for a coin buried under the sand. A hammerhead shark does almost the same thing. The difference is that the detector is its own head. The wide, flat head is called a cephalofoil. Underneath it are hundreds of tiny pits filled with jelly, and those pits can sense electricity. Every living animal leaks a faint electric signal, even one lying perfectly still. A stingray can bury itself until only its eyes show, and it is still shouting in a language the hammerhead can hear. So the shark cruises low over the seafloor, swinging its head in slow arcs. The wider the head, the wider the sweep. When the signal grows strong, the shark stops swinging and starts digging. A great hammerhead has one more move. It slams the flat of its head down on the stingray, pins it to the sand, and takes a bite from the edge of the wing. The head is a tool, and the shark knows exactly how to use it.

blocks.prompt: Built Wide on Purpose
blocks.text: Most sharks are shaped like torpedoes, and for good reason. A smooth, pointed body slides through water with almost no drag. Then there is the hammerhead, swimming around with a head stretched sideways like a set of handlebars. It looks like a mistake. It is not. The head has a name, the cephalofoil, and it does at least two jobs at once. The first job is seeing. A hammerhead's eyes sit on the far tips of the head, as far apart as they can possibly get. Scientists once assumed this was a problem, because the head must block the view straight ahead. They tested it, and the opposite turned out to be true. The wide spacing gives the shark overlapping vision in front and a nearly complete circle of vision above and below. A hammerhead can watch the surface and the seafloor at the same instant. The second job is feeling. Sharks have organs called ampullae of Lorenzini, small pores filled with jelly that detect the faint electric fields every living body produces. All sharks have them. The hammerhead simply has more room to spread them out. Its head is a search coil, and it sweeps that coil across the sand in slow arcs the way a person sweeps a metal detector. A stingray buried under an inch of sand is invisible and silent, but it cannot switch off its own heartbeat. The hammerhead reads it, drops, and pins the ray flat with its head. Wide costs the shark something. Drag is real, and the head is heavy to swing. But a shark that finds food nobody else can find has already won the trade.

blocks.prompt: The Case for a Ridiculous Head
blocks.text: Evolution is not a designer. It has no plan and no taste. It keeps whatever survives long enough to have babies, and it throws out the rest. Which makes the hammerhead shark a genuinely good puzzle, because at first glance its head looks like something evolution should have thrown out. The rest of the shark is a masterpiece of low drag. The head is a wing bolted on sideways. That head is called a cephalofoil, and it is younger than you might expect. Hammerheads split from other sharks somewhere around twenty million years ago, which makes them recent arrivals in a family line that stretches back hundreds of millions of years. So the head is not ancient baggage. It is a new idea that worked. Here is what it buys. First, vision. The eyes sit at the outermost tips, and researchers who actually measured the field of view found that hammerheads see better forward than pointed-nosed sharks do, not worse. The eyes overlap in front, giving depth perception, and the vertical field is close to a full circle. Second, electroreception. Every shark carries ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores that read the electric fields leaking from living tissue. A hammerhead has the same organ spread across a much broader plate, so each sweep of the head scans a wider corridor of seafloor. A stingray buried in sand is invisible, motionless, and completely exposed, because a heartbeat cannot be hidden. Third, and this one is strange: great hammerheads do not swim upright. Video studies found them cruising rolled onto their side, sometimes by as much as seventy degrees, using that tall dorsal fin as a lift surface. Rolling over cuts their drag by around ten percent. The shark solved its own drag problem by lying down. None of this saved them. Scalloped and great hammerheads are now critically endangered. Their fins are large and valuable, they gather in predictable schools of hundreds around seamounts, and they die faster than almost any other shark once caught. A body built to find what nothing else can find is no defense against a net.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Sphyrnidae; the head is a cephalofoil
Diverged from other sharks roughly 20 million years ago
Ampullae of Lorenzini read electric fields in the sand
Great hammerheads swim rolled up to 70 degrees to cut drag
Scalloped hammerheads close their gills on deep cold dives
The bonnethead digests seagrass, the only known omnivorous shark

blocks.prompt: The Argument the Hammerhead Makes
blocks.text: Evolution has no foresight. It cannot plan, cannot sketch, cannot decide that a shape would look impressive. It only keeps what survives long enough to reproduce and discards everything else, slowly and without sentiment. That is what makes the hammerhead shark such a useful animal to argue with. Every other line of the shark's body obeys the rule that water punishes anything wide. Then, at the front, evolution bolted on a wing turned sideways. The structure is called a cephalofoil, and the first thing worth knowing about it is its age. Hammerheads separated from the other sharks roughly twenty million years ago, which sounds enormous until you set it beside a lineage over four hundred million years old. In shark terms, hammerheads are new. The head is not leftover history that nobody has cleaned up. It is a recent experiment that paid for itself, and a fair test of the idea that anything expensive must be earning its keep. It earns it in three ways. The first is sight. The eyes sit at the outermost tips of the head, which for decades was assumed to be a cost: surely that slab of flesh blocks the view straight ahead. Researchers eventually stopped assuming and measured it, recording the actual visual fields, and found that hammerheads have better forward vision than pointed-nosed sharks, not worse. The eyes overlap in front for depth perception, and the vertical field approaches a complete circle. The animal can watch the surface and the seafloor in the same moment. The second is electroreception. All sharks carry ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores that read the faint electric fields leaking from living tissue. The hammerhead did not invent a new sense. It simply spread an old one across a wider plate and swings it. A stingray buried under an inch of sand is invisible, motionless, and utterly exposed, because a heartbeat cannot be switched off. The great hammerhead then drives the flat of its head down onto the ray and pins it to the bottom. The third is the strangest, because the shark appears to have solved its own drag problem by cheating. Great hammerheads do not swim upright. Video tracking caught them cruising rolled onto their side, sometimes as far as seventy degrees, using their unusually tall dorsal fin as a lift surface instead of the pectoral fins. Rolled over, they cut drag by roughly ten percent. An animal shaped like a mistake found a posture that made the mistake cheaper. And none of it matters. Scalloped and great hammerheads are now listed as critically endangered. Their fins are large and command high prices. They aggregate in schools of hundreds around the same seamounts year after year, which is precisely what a fishing fleet needs. Worse, they are physiologically fragile once caught: their stress response is severe enough that many die on the line before anyone decides whether to release them. Twenty million years of refinement produced a sensor array so good it can hear a heart beating through sand, and it offers no defense whatsoever against a net that simply waits in a place the shark cannot stop returning to. Evolution optimizes for the last problem, not the next one.
